title: Class 6 Maths Practical Geometry: Ruler & Compass Constructions + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn Class 6 maths practical geometry: ruler-and-compass steps for circles, segments, perpendiculars and angles, with case studies and a free quiz.
excerpt: The Practical Geometry chapter is where a compass stops being a toy and starts doing real work. Here are the exact construction steps for Class 6, two solved case studies, and a quiz to test yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 6 student a compass for the first time and something odd happens — they treat it like a weapon, not a tool. The class 6 maths practical geometry chapter fixes that. It is the first time in the NCERT syllabus that children build shapes exactly, using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, with no measuring of angles by protractor guesswork. Every line, every arc, every point has a reason. That is what makes this chapter satisfying to teach: there is a right way, and when you follow the steps, the figure is simply correct.

In my experience the students who struggle here are not weak at maths — they are rushing. They swing the compass before setting the radius, or they lift it mid-arc so the width slips. So before any construction, one rule: set the compass, lock your grip, and do not let the hinge move until the arc is done.

What the Class 6 practical geometry chapter actually covers

The chapter is a fixed list of constructions. Nothing exotic, but each one builds on the last, so the order matters. Here is the full set you are expected to do with a ruler and compass alone.

  • A circle of a given radius
  • A line segment of a given length, and a copy of a segment
  • A perpendicular to a line through a point on it
  • A perpendicular to a line from a point outside it
  • The perpendicular bisector of a line segment
  • Angles of 60°, 120°, 90°, 30° and 45°
  • The bisector of a given angle

The two tools, and what each is for

The ruler draws straight lines and measures length. The compass does everything else — it carries a fixed distance from one place to another. That second idea is the whole secret of the chapter. When you copy a segment or strike equal arcs, you are really just carrying one length around the page without a scale. Once a child sees the compass as a ‘distance carrier’ rather than a circle-drawer, the rest clicks.

Step-by-step: the core constructions

Drawing a circle of given radius

Say the radius is 4 cm. Open the compass against a ruler until the pencil tip sits exactly on 4 cm from the needle. Press the needle at your chosen centre O, hold the top of the compass, and turn the pencil in one smooth sweep. The distance from O to every point on the curve is 4 cm — that is the definition of a circle, made visible.

Copying a line segment

To copy a segment AB onto a new line: draw a working line and mark a start point P on it. Set the compass width to exactly AB by placing the needle on A and the pencil on B. Without changing that width, place the needle on P and strike an arc cutting the line at Q. PQ now equals AB, with no ruler needed for the transfer.

Perpendicular bisector of a segment

This is the workhorse construction. With segment AB:

  • Open the compass to more than half of AB.
  • With the needle on A, draw arcs above and below the line.
  • Keep the same width, put the needle on B, and draw two more arcs crossing the first pair.
  • Join the two crossing points. That line is perpendicular to AB and cuts it exactly in half.

Constructing a 60° angle, then 30° by bisecting

Draw a ray OA. With the needle on O, draw a wide arc cutting OA at a point, call it P. Without changing the width, put the needle on P and cut the arc at Q. Join OQ — angle AOQ is exactly 60°, because you have effectively built one corner of an equilateral triangle. To get 30°, bisect that 60° angle: from P and Q strike equal arcs that cross, then join O to the crossing point.

How the standard angles are built

Notice that you never measure a single angle with a protractor. Each one comes from arcs and bisection. This table shows how the exam-standard angles relate.

AngleHow it is builtBuilt from
60°One arc-step on a circleEquilateral idea
120°Two arc-steps on the same circle60° + 60°
90°Perpendicular, or bisect 60° and 120°Perpendicular / arcs
30°Bisect a 60° angle60°
45°Bisect a 90° angle90°

Case study 1: fencing a circular garden bed

Meera’s father marks the centre of a round flower bed in their Nagpur backyard and wants a border exactly 4 cm from the centre on her scale drawing. On paper, she must construct a circle of radius 4 cm and then mark a point on the boundary where the tap pipe will meet it at a right angle.

Solution. First she sets her compass to 4 cm against the ruler and draws the circle with centre O. Next she draws a radius OA to the boundary. To make the pipe meet the circle at 90°, she constructs a perpendicular to OA at point A: with the needle on A she marks two equal points on the radius line, then from those two points strikes crossing arcs and joins them through A. The pipe line is now perpendicular to the radius — which, as a bonus, means it is a tangent to the circle at A.

Case study 2: the notice board and the 120° bracket

A carpenter needs to fix two support brackets on a wall meeting at 120°. Rohan is asked to draw the angle accurately for the plan using only a ruler and compass.

Solution. He draws a ray OA and, with the needle on O, sweeps a wide arc cutting OA at P. Keeping the width fixed, he steps the compass along the arc: from P to a new point Q, then from Q to R. Joining OR gives 120°, because each step is a 60° arc and two steps make 120°. To check, he bisects the angle — the bisector should read 60° on each side. This is exactly the kind of reasoning the case-study questions reward: not just the figure, but why each arc lands where it does.

Try the quiz, then the case-study workbook

The eight questions below check the ideas that trip students up most — radius, copying lengths, which angles bisect into which, and the perpendicular bisector. Attempt each one, then read the explanation for anything you miss. When you want longer, exam-style practice, the printable case-study workbook at the end gives passage-based constructions with full solved steps, so you can see the reasoning laid out the way examiners expect.

quiz.title: Class 6 Practical Geometry Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on circles, line segments, perpendiculars and standard angles. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which two tools does practical geometry in Class 6 use for constructions?
questions.explanation: Class 6 constructions are done using only a ruler (for straight lines and length) and a pair of compasses (to carry a fixed distance).

questions.q: To draw a circle of radius 5 cm, where do you set the compass width?
options: To 5 cm from needle to pencil
questions.explanation: The compass width equals the radius, so the pencil sits exactly 5 cm from the needle point.

questions.q: When you bisect a 60° angle, what angle do you get?
questions.explanation: Bisecting means cutting in half, so half of 60° is 30°.

questions.q: A 120° angle is built by stepping how many 60° arcs along the same circle?
questions.explanation: Each arc-step is 60°, so two steps give 60° + 60° = 120°.

questions.q: The perpendicular bisector of a segment AB does what?
options: Cuts AB in half at a right angle
Passes through only one end of AB
questions.explanation: A perpendicular bisector crosses AB at 90° and divides it into two equal parts.

questions.q: To copy a segment AB onto a new line, you should
options: Set the compass to AB, then strike an arc from the new start point
questions.explanation: Setting the compass to AB and striking an arc carries the exact length to the new line without a scale.

questions.q: Which angle is made by bisecting a 90° angle?
questions.explanation: Half of 90° is 45°, so bisecting a right angle gives 45°.

questions.q: Before setting the compass, what must you open it against to draw a segment of exact length?
questions.explanation: You open the compass against the ruler scale so the needle-to-pencil distance matches the required length.

faq.q: What is practical geometry in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: It is the chapter where you construct exact figures — circles, line segments, perpendiculars, perpendicular bisectors and standard angles — using only a ruler and a pair of compasses, without measuring angles by protractor.

faq.q: Which angles can be constructed with only a compass and ruler?
faq.a: The standard ones in the NCERT chapter are 60°, 120°, 90°, 30° and 45°. Each is built from arcs and bisection — for example 30° by bisecting 60°, and 45° by bisecting 90°.

faq.q: Why can I not use a protractor for these constructions?
faq.a: The point of the chapter is exactness through geometry, not measurement. A protractor reading can be off by a degree or two; arcs struck with a fixed compass width are precise every time.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake students make?
faq.a: Changing the compass width mid-construction. If the hinge slips between arcs, the figure is wrong. Set the width, hold your grip, and complete the arc before adjusting anything.
